summary: Provides the framework for dynamic provisioning of MPLS-TP transport paths using a control plane, covering addressing, routing, path computation, signaling, traffic engineering, and recovery. MPLS-TP uses GMPLS as its control plane. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS-TP is a profile of MPLS designed to behave like a traditional transport network: paths are set up, checked and restored as a whole. This memo says how a network should do that automatically, by reusing the signalling and routing that GMPLS and LDP already provide.

questions: how do you set up mpls-tp paths dynamically
subtitle: Framework for automatic provisioning of MPLS Transport Profile paths.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TP can be set up by hand from a management system, but the requirements ask for paths to be built automatically by a control plane, and no such control plane existed.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the framework: GMPLS handles the label switched paths, the existing pseudowire control plane handles the pseudowires, and the requirements are traced to the mechanisms that satisfy them, with the extensions still needed listed.
tldr.outcome: It is a framework, not a specification. It says which existing protocols to reuse, which requirements they already meet, and where new work is needed.

facts.label: Control plane used for pseudowires
facts.value: The pseudowire control plane, based on targeted LDP

today: RFC 6373 is an Informational document from September 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a framework: it names the protocols to reuse and lists the extensions that were still needed, and it is not itself a specification an implementation would follow.

sections.title: What the Document Covers and the Approach It Takes
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile is defined as a joint effort between the International Telecommunication Union and the IETF. The requirements for MPLS-TP are defined in the requirements document, RFC 5654, which state that a solution must be defined to support dynamic provisioning of MPLS-TP transport paths via a control plane. This document provides the framework for such dynamic provisioning, covering control-plane addressing, routing, path computation, signalling, traffic engineering and path recovery. MPLS-TP uses GMPLS as the control plane for MPLS-TP label switched paths, and also uses the pseudowire control plane for pseudowires. Management-plane functions are out of scope.

The scope is the control-plane functions involved in establishing MPLS-TP label switched paths and pseudowires. The LSPs provided by MPLS-TP are used as a server layer for IP, MPLS and pseudowires, as well as other tunnelled MPLS-TP LSPs. The pseudowires are used to carry client signals other than IP or MPLS, and the relationship between them is exactly the same as between pseudowires and MPLS LSPs in an MPLS packet switched network. MPLS-TP also defines protection and restoration functions, and the control plane provides methods to establish, remove and control LSPs and pseudowires, which includes control of operations, administration and maintenance functions, data-plane functions and recovery functions.

The basic approach taken in defining the framework is that MPLS technology as defined by the IETF is the foundation; the data plane for MPLS-TP is a standard MPLS data plane as profiled in RFC 5960; MPLS pseudowires are used including targeted LDP as the foundation for pseudowire signalling, with OSPF-TE, IS-IS TE or MP-BGP as they apply for multi-segment pseudowire routing; the LSP control plane builds on the GMPLS control plane, whose protocols in scope are RSVP-TE, OSPF-TE and IS-IS TE; existing IETF MPLS and GMPLS documents and evolving working group drafts should be reused wherever possible; extensions should first be based on existing and evolving IETF work, and only secondly on work by other standards bodies when the IETF decides that work is out of its scope; extensions may be required to fully automate functions related to MPLS-TP LSPs and pseudowires; control-plane software upgrades to existing equipment are acceptable and expected; it is permissible for functions present in the GMPLS and pseudowire control planes not to be used in MPLS-TP networks; one possible use of the control plane is to configure, enable and generally control OAM functionality, which will require extensions to existing control-plane specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan is to build the new transport network out of pieces that already exist. The paths are ordinary MPLS label switched paths, signalled with RSVP-TE and routed with the traffic engineering extensions to OSPF or IS-IS, which is what the GMPLS control plane already is. The pseudowires keep the LDP control plane they have always had, and anything else is spelled out as new work.

sections.title: The Reference Model
sections.content:
The control-plane reference model is based on the general MPLS-TP reference model as defined in the MPLS-TP framework (RFC 5921) and further refined in RFC 6215 on the User-to-Network and Network-to-Network Interfaces. The MPLS-TP control plane is based on GMPLS with RSVP-TE for LSP signalling and targeted LDP for pseudowire signalling. In both cases, OSPF-TE or IS-IS TE with GMPLS extensions is used for dynamic routing within an MPLS-TP domain. Here, targeted LDP means LDP as defined in RFC 5036, using targeted hello messages.

From a service perspective, MPLS-TP client services may be supported via both pseudowires and LSPs. Pseudowire client interfaces, or adaptations, are defined on an interface-technology basis, for example Ethernet over pseudowire. In the context of an MPLS-TP LSP, the client interface is provided at the network layer and may be controlled via a GMPLS-based UNI, or statically provisioned. MPLS-TP also presumes an NNI reference point.

The end-to-end control-plane reference model shows the control-plane protocols used by MPLS-TP, as well as the UNI and NNI reference points, in the case of a single-segment pseudowire supported by an end-to-end LSP without any hierarchical LSPs. Each service provider node's participation in routing and signalling, both GMPLS RSVP-TE and pseudowire LDP, is represented. Only the service end points participate in pseudowire LDP signalling, while all service provider nodes participate in GMPLS traffic engineering LSP routing and signalling. A second model adds three hierarchical LSP segments. These segments are present to support scaling, OAM and Maintenance Entity Group End Points within each provider domain and across the inter-provider NNI. The end points are used to collect performance information, support diagnostic and fault management functions, and support OAM-triggered survivability schemes. Each hierarchical LSP may be protected or restored using any of the schemes discussed in the survivability framework. End-to-end monitoring is supported via end points at the end-to-end LSP and pseudowire end points.

While not shown in the figures, the MPLS-TP control plane must support the addressing separation and independence between the data, control and management planes. Address separation between the planes is already included in GMPLS, and is also already included in LDP, since LDP session end point addresses are never automatically associated with forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: The picture is a row of provider routers with customer routers at each end. The LSP runs the whole way across and is set up and routed by every provider in the path. The pseudowire is different: only the two end points speak about it, and the providers in between just carry it. Hierarchical LSPs break the long path into segments so each provider can check and restore its own piece.

sections.title: The Control-Plane Requirements
sections.content:
The requirements for the MPLS-TP control plane are derived from the MPLS-TP requirements and framework documents, specifically RFC 5654, RFC 5921, RFC 5860, RFC 6371 and RFC 6372. The requirements are summarized in that section but do not replace those documents, and if there are differences the other documents are authoritative.

The primary requirements cover the behaviour the control plane has to have. Among them, the control plane must support the establishment of MPLS-TP LSPs and pseudowires, must support both single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires, and must support the control of pseudowires and LSPs. The requirements also state that GMPLS RSVP-TE and related extensions are used for LSP signalling, and GMPLS OSPF-TE and IS-IS TE are used for routing.

The identifier requirements are based on RFC 6370. The control plane must support MPLS-TP point-to-point tunnel identifiers of the forms defined there, MPLS-TP LSP identifiers of the forms defined there together with their mappings to GMPLS, pseudowire path identifiers, Maintenance Entity Group identifiers for LSPs and pseudowires, IP-compatible Maintenance Entity Group identifiers, and Maintenance Entity Group End Point identifiers of the forms defined for LSPs and pseudowires, including IP-based forms for LSPs and for pseudowires.

A separate set of requirements is derived from the OAM framework, and the document has a separate section on security requirements, which records that there are no specific MPLS-TP control-plane security requirements beyond those of the MPLS and GMPLS security framework, and that the document defining the security framework applies equally to MPLS-TP.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements are not written from scratch. They are pulled from the documents that define what MPLS-TP is meant to do, and then numbered one to one hundred and forty-three. The identifiers section is important in practice: every path, pseudowire and maintenance entity needs a name that every element in the network agrees on, and those names come from a separate specification.

sections.title: The LSP Control Plane and the GMPLS Functions It Uses
sections.content:
MPLS-TP uses Generalized MPLS signalling and routing as the control plane for LSPs. The GMPLS control plane is based on the MPLS control plane, and includes support for MPLS labelled data and transport data planes, so it includes most of the transport-centric features required to support MPLS-TP LSPs.

On addressing, MPLS-TP reuses and supports the addressing mechanisms supported by MPLS, and the identifiers document provides additional context on how IP addresses are used. MPLS, and consequently MPLS-TP, uses the IPv4 and IPv6 address families to identify MPLS-TP nodes by default for network management and signalling purposes. The address spaces and neighbour adjacencies in the control, management and data planes may be completely separated or combined at the discretion of the operator and based on the equipment capabilities of a vendor. The separation of the control and management planes from the data plane allows each plane to be independently addressable, each plane may use addresses that are not mutually reachable, and each may use a different address family.

Routing support for MPLS-TP LSPs is based on GMPLS routing, which builds on traffic engineering routing and has been extended to support multiple switching technologies as well as multiple levels of packet switching within a single network. IS-IS extensions for GMPLS build on the traffic engineering extensions to IS-IS, and OSPF extensions for GMPLS build on the traffic engineering extensions to OSPF.

Both MPLS and GMPLS allow traffic engineering and constraint-based path computation. MPLS path computation provides paths for unidirectional point-to-point and point-to-multipoint LSPs, and GMPLS path computation adds bidirectional LSPs, explicit recovery path computation, and other functions. Both allow the restriction of path selection based on the use of Explicit Route Objects and other LSP attributes. No specific algorithm is standardized by the IETF, and this is anticipated to continue for MPLS-TP LSPs. Path Computation Element based approaches may be used for path computation of a GMPLS LSP across domains and within a single domain, using the PCE Communication Protocol, although MPLS-TP-specific extensions to that protocol are currently out of scope.

GMPLS signalling is based on RSVP-TE, and all RSVP-TE extensions that apply to MPLS may also be used for GMPLS and consequently MPLS-TP, most notably the support for point-to-multipoint signalling. Constraint-based Routed LDP is no longer under active development and is deprecated, and must not be used for MPLS or MPLS-TP. Support for unnumbered links is permitted, at the discretion of the operator, and link bundling may also be used.

Hierarchical LSPs are reused from earlier work. Signalling mechanisms allow a hierarchical LSP to be treated as a single hop in the path of another LSP, and a Forwarding Adjacency is a data link created from an LSP and advertised in the same instance of the control plane that advertises the traffic engineering links from which the LSP is constructed. LSP hierarchy is expected to play an important role in MPLS-TP networks, particularly in the context of scaling and recovery.

GMPLS defines extensions in support of end-to-end recovery and segment recovery, with segment recovery providing a superset of the end-to-end function. The five defined types of recovery are 1+1 bidirectional protection for point-to-point LSPs, 1+1 unidirectional protection for point-to-multipoint LSPs, 1:n protection with or without extra traffic, rerouting without extra traffic including shared mesh restoration, and full LSP rerouting. The use of notify messages to trigger protection switching and recovery is not required in MPLS-TP, as this function is expected to be supported via OAM, though its use is not precluded. Finally, while most GMPLS control-plane documents define the control plane from the point of view of an internal network-to-network interface, some operators may deploy signalled interfaces across user-to-network interfaces and across inter-provider external network-to-network interfaces, which may require extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece of GMPLS is examined to see whether MPLS-TP can simply use it. Addressing, routing with the traffic engineering extensions, constraint-based path computation with explicit routes, and RSVP-TE signalling all work as they are, including the point-to-multipoint signalling. Recovery comes in five shapes, from duplicating the path to rerouting it, and MPLS-TP uses the ones already defined rather than inventing a new one.

sections.title: Pseudowires and Their Control Plane
sections.content:
MPLS pseudowires are defined in RFC 3985 and RFC 5659, and provide emulated services over an MPLS packet switched network. Several types have been defined: Ethernet pseudowires for Ethernet port or VLAN transport, HDLC and PPP pseudowires, ATM pseudowires, Frame Relay pseudowires, and circuit emulation pseudowires. Today's transport networks based on Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy, WDM or SONET provide transport for those client signals with no payload awareness, and implementing pseudowire capability allows an existing technology to substitute the time-division multiplexing transport with packet-based transport, providing potentially better bandwidth utilization.

There are two general classes of pseudowire: single-segment pseudowires and multi-segment pseudowires. An MPLS-TP network domain may transparently transport a pseudowire whose end points are within a client network. Alternatively, an MPLS-TP edge node may be the terminating provider edge for a pseudowire, performing adaptation from the native attachment circuit technology to an MPLS pseudowire that is then transported in an LSP over an MPLS-TP network. In this way the pseudowire is analogous to a transport channel in a time-division multiplexing network, and the LSP is equivalent to a container of multiple non-concatenated channels, albeit they are packet containers. An MPLS-TP network may also contain switching provider edges for a multi-segment pseudowire, whereby the terminating provider edges may be at the edge of an MPLS-TP network or in a client network, in which case a terminating provider edge in a client network performs the adaptation of the native service to MPLS and the MPLS-TP network performs pseudowire switching.

The single-segment pseudowire signalling control plane is based on targeted LDP, with specific procedures defined in RFC 4447, and the multi-segment pseudowire signalling control plane is also based on targeted LDP. An MPLS-TP network shall use the same pseudowire signalling protocols and procedures for placing single-segment and multi-segment pseudowires, which leverages existing technology and facilitates interoperability with client networks that have native attachment circuits or pseudowire segments switched across an MPLS-TP network. There is no MPLS-TP requirement for a standardized management interface to the MPLS-TP control plane.

The relationship between the pseudowire and LSP control planes in MPLS-TP is the same as the relationship found in the PWE3 maintenance reference model. Pseudowire control takes place separately from LSP signalling, and the two control planes may be used independently, with one employed without the other. This translates into four possible scenarios: no control plane is employed; a control plane is used for both LSPs and pseudowires; a control plane is used for LSPs but not pseudowires; or a control plane is used for pseudowires but not LSPs. The main coordination between LSP and pseudowire control occurs within the nodes that terminate pseudowires or pseudowire segments. Extending RSVP-TE to support pseudowire control is out of scope, so the control of pseudowires and LSPs will operate largely independently.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire carries one client service, such as an Ethernet circuit, across the packet network as if it were a dedicated line. There are two kinds: one that crosses the network in a single hop, and one that can be switched in the middle, and both are signalled with targeted LDP. The control of a pseudowire is separate from the control of the LSP that carries it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document primarily describes how existing mechanisms can be used to meet the MPLS-TP control-plane requirements, and the documents that describe each mechanism contain their own security considerations sections. For a general discussion of MPLS and GMPLS related security issues, the MPLS and GMPLS security framework applies. As mentioned earlier, there are no specific MPLS-TP control-plane security requirements. The document also identifies a number of needed control-plane extensions, and it is expected that the documents that define such extensions will also include any appropriate security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new: the security rules of the protocols being reused apply unchanged, and the new extensions will carry their own security sections when they are written.

layers.detail: Signalled and routed by every provider on the path

viz.caption: THE PIECES OF THE PSEUDOWIRE MODEL

items.title: Single-segment pseudowire
items.text: A client service carried end to end across the network in one hop, signalled with targeted LDP.

items.title: Multi-segment pseudowire
items.text: A client service whose segments may be switched in the middle of the network.

items.title: Terminating provider edge
items.text: The edge node that adapts the native attachment circuit to an MPLS pseudowire.

items.title: Switching provider edge
items.text: A node that switches a pseudowire segment without terminating the client service.

items.title: Four control-plane combinations
items.text: No control plane, both, LSPs only, or pseudowires only. The two control planes may be used independently.
